claim: CRA (Reg. (EU) 2024/2847) applies from 2027-12-11; Article 14 (reporting) applies from 2026-09-11; Chapter IV (notified bodies) from 2026-06-11 (Art. 71(2)).

CRA Art. 13(8): support period must reflect expected use time and be at least five years (shorter only if expected use is shorter); factors include the support periods of integrated third-party components providing core functions and the availability of the operating environment.
CRA Art. 13(9): each security update made available during the support period must remain available for at least 10 years after issue or the remainder of the support period, whichever is longer.

CRA Art. 13(10): for subsequent substantially modified versions of a software product, the manufacturer may meet Annex I Part II(2) only for the latest version, provided users of earlier versions get the latest version free of charge and without extra cost to adjust their hardware/software environment.
CRA Art. 13(19): the end date of the support period (at least month and year) must be clearly specified at the time of purchase; where feasible users are notified when support ends.
CRA Art. 13(23): a manufacturer that ceases operations must inform market surveillance authorities and, as far as possible, users before cessation takes effect.

CRA Art. 14(1)-(2),(8): actively exploited vulnerabilities must be notified via the ENISA single reporting platform: early warning within 24 h, vulnerability notification within 72 h, final report within 14 days after a fix is available; impacted users must be informed.

CRA Annex I Part I(2)(c): products must ensure vulnerabilities can be addressed through security updates, including, where applicable, automatic security updates enabled as a default setting with a clear and easy opt-out, notification of updates, and the option to temporarily postpone them.

CRA Annex I Part I(2): secure-by-default configuration including reset to original state (b); confidentiality incl. encryption at rest/in transit (e); integrity (f); attack-surface limitation (j); logging with opt-out (l); secure permanent removal of all data and settings (m).

CRA Annex I Part II: SBOM in a commonly used machine-readable format covering at least top-level dependencies (1); security updates separate from functionality updates where technically feasible (2); coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy (5); security updates free of charge with advisories (8).

CRA Annex III lists 'Operating systems' (Class I, item 11), 'Boot managers' (I-8), VPN products (I-5), routers (I-12), identity management systems (I-1) and smart home general purpose virtual assistants (I-16); Class II includes 'Hypervisors and container runtime systems'.

CRA Art. 32(2): a Class I important product whose manufacturer has not applied (or only partly applied) harmonised standards, common specifications or an EU certification scheme must use EU-type examination (module B+C) or full quality assurance (module H), i.e. a notified body.

CRA Art. 32(5): manufacturers of products qualifying as free and open-source software in Annex III categories may use any Art. 32(1) procedure, including internal control (module A), provided the technical documentation is made public when the product is placed on the market.

CRA Art. 3: 'manufacturer' covers products marketed under its name whether for payment, monetisation or free of charge; an 'open-source software steward' is a legal person other than a manufacturer; recital 15 says intention to monetise, e.g. via a platform through which other services are monetised, indicates commercial activity.
CRA Art. 21-22: an importer or distributor placing a product under its own name/trademark, or anyone carrying out a substantial modification and making it available, is treated as a manufacturer.
CRA Art. 69(2)-(3): products placed on the market before 2027-12-11 are subject only if substantially modified afterwards, but Art. 14 reporting applies to all in-scope products regardless.

Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2392 (28 Nov 2025, OJ 1.12.2025) defines 'operating systems' as software that abstracts hardware and controls execution of software, and 'container runtime systems' as software managing execution and lifecycle of containers on a single host OS; classification follows the product's core functionality, and integrating a component does not by itself change the class.

ETSI (13 Aug 2026) put 17 CRA vertical final-draft standards into Public Enquiry closing mid-Sept to mid-Nov 2026; they are intended to become harmonised standards giving presumption of conformity; no publication/citation date given.

Draft ETSI EN 304 626 V1.0.1 (2026-08, enquiry draft, Operating Systems) requires a secure update mechanism operating by default with an easy opt-out (MI-KEVA), update authenticity/integrity verification (MI-SUVI), a monotonic anti-rollback counter (MI-SUDP), explicit authorisation for user-initiated rollback with automated recovery after failed update exempt (MI-SUAR), and a default option to encrypt stored user data (MI-ENST).

RED Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, as amended by (EU) 2023/2444, applies from 1 August 2025: Art. 3(3)(d) to internet-connected radio equipment, (e) to equipment processing personal/traffic/location data, (f) to equipment enabling money transfers.
Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/138 cites EN 18031-1/-2/-3:2024 with restrictions: no presumption of conformity where the user is allowed not to set and use any password (clauses 6.2.5.1/6.2.5.2).
Debian 13 trixie: LTS period 2028-08-09 to 2030-06-30; LTS architecture list 'to be determined'.
Freexian ELTS lists Debian 13 Trixie until 2035-06-30, covering 'at least amd64, others can be added on request'; prices are by quote and not published.
NIST CMVP: FIPS 140-2 validations moved to the Historical List on 21/22 September 2026; CMVP still supports purchase and use of historical modules for existing systems.
RKE2 FIPS documentation describes FIPS 140-2 only and links BoringCrypto CMVP certificate #4407 as the validated module used by its FIPS Go compiler.

CMVP #4735 BoringCrypto (version 2022061300) is FIPS 140-3 Active, validated 2024-07-23, sunset 2029-07-22; tested OEs are Android 13 Pixels, Debian 'Rodete' and Google Prodimage.

CJIS Security Policy v6.1 (2026-06-25) SC-13: CJI in transit outside a physically secure location needs FIPS 140-3 certified modules OR FIPS 197 AES with at least 256-bit keys; 'FIPS 140-2 certificates will not be acceptable after September 21, 2026'; SC-28 sets the same choice for CJI at rest.

COPPA Rule 16 CFR 312.2 defines an 'operator' as a person operating a website or online service who collects or maintains personal information from or about its users; Part 312 sections carry 2025-06-23 amendment dates in eCFR.
16 CFR 312.8(b) (amended): operators must keep a written information security program, designate a coordinator, and perform risk assessments at least annually.

GDPR Art. 2(2)(c) excludes purely personal or household processing, but recital 18 keeps controllers/processors that provide the means for such processing in scope; Art. 8 sets 16 as the default age for consent to information society services (Member States may lower to 13).
California CPPA: updated CCPA regulations (ADMT, risk assessments, cybersecurity audits) approved by OAL and filed on 2025-09-22, effective 2026-01-01.
47 CFR 15.101(a): Class B personal computers and other Class B digital devices must be authorized by SDoC or Certification before marketing.
47 CFR 8.203(k): the FCC IoT Labeling (Cyber Trust Mark) program is voluntary.

UK PSTI security requirements (SI 2023/1007) in force 29 April 2024: password rules, published vulnerability reporting, and a published 'defined support period'; desktop and laptop computers and non-cellular tablets are excepted.

AI Act Art. 113: general application 2026-08-02; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI, OJ 2026-07-24) sets 2027-12-02 for Annex III high-risk systems and 2028-08-02 for Annex I (product-safety) high-risk systems.

Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 14 January 2027 (Art. 54); Annex III 1.1.9 requires protection against corruption, identification of safety-critical software, and evidence of legitimate or illegitimate software intervention.
Microsoft: KEK CA 2011 expires 2026-06-24, UEFI CA 2011 expires 2026-06-27 (replaced by UEFI CA 2023 and Option ROM UEFI CA 2023), Windows Production PCA 2011 expires 2026-10-19.

Microsoft (2026-06-24): after the 2011 CA expires Microsoft can only sign shims with the 2023 CA; systems whose firmware db lacks the 2023 CA fail to boot a 2023-only shim; do not remove the 2011 CA from db.

Debian supports Secure Boot via Microsoft-signed shim since Debian 10; DKMS modules must be signed with an enrolled MOK; Secure Boot enables kernel lockdown which blocks unsigned modules; from trixie systemd-boot can be used with shim as an opt-in.

systemd-cryptenroll: --tpm2-public-key binds to a signed PCR policy (default PCR 11, any UKI with a valid PCR signature) so measurements can change on every update while signatures stay valid; literal --tpm2-pcrs binding breaks after updates; PCRs 7, 11 and 14 (with shim/MOK) are the general recommendation; --tpm2-pcrlock since systemd 255.

Rugix (rugix/rugix@c2f5f4f) has a data-partition driver 'luks2-tpm2' that seals a LUKS2 key with systemd-cryptenroll; the driver config is marked #[unstable] and warns that binding PCRs 0-9 bricks devices on update, with TPM2_PolicyAuthorize (tpm2-public-key) planned for a future revision; feature added 2026-05-09 (commit 707b2fd).
Rugix has a systemd-boot boot flow using LoaderEntryDefault/LoaderEntryOneShot via bootctl, and ships a partition schema 'systemd-boot-system' of EFI (512M), system-a, system-b, data.
Rugix v1.4.0 (2026-11-02) preserves prepared boot partition contents in the rpi-tryboot and rpi-uboot flows when boot.img is present, 'keeping authenticated boot images unchanged'.
umbrelOS x86 images use Rugix target generic-grub-efi with a 256M FAT 'config' ESP and ext4 boot partitions; umbrelOS states it does not use Secure Boot and leaves DKMS modules unsigned.

umbrelOS exposes an MCP tool install_os_update that, after assertSystemAccess, installs the available OS update in the background and auto-restarts the device; the only safety signal is the destructiveHint annotation.

HAOS builds RAUC bundles with format=verity; a code search of home-assistant/operating-system@ab7d0f1 found no Secure Boot key enrolment, TPM sealing or LUKS data encryption in the HAOS image (only kernel options and vendor Amlogic boot loaders).

HA Supervisor computes an add-on/app security rating of 1-8: +1 for an AppArmor profile, -1 if AppArmor disabled, +2 for ingress, +1 if signed, -1 for dangerous capabilities, -1/-2 for manager/admin API roles, and forced to 1 for Docker API or full access.
Olares' add-node script downloads an AppArmor .deb from Launchpad with curl -k (TLS verification disabled) and installs it with dpkg -i.

Raspberry Pi secure boot: boot ROM verifies against a hash of the customer RSA-2048 public key in OTP; on BCM2712 the customer key also signs the EEPROM bootloader; the bootloader verifies boot.img with boot.sig; an OTP device-unique secret unlocks a LUKS root (AES-XTS on BCM2712).

Raspberry Pi bootloader: if secure-boot is enabled, tryboot loads tryboot.img instead of boot.img, and tryboot_a_b is implicitly set when loading files from within a boot.img ramdisk (partition-level A/B).

Raspberry Pi docs: 'Raspberry Pi computers do not have a hardware protected key store'; rpi-sb-provisioner: generating the BCM2712 device key 'writes to OTP permanently and cannot be undone'; JTAG lock and signing-key programming are irreversible.

Jetson Orin secure boot (r36.4.4): the OEM generates PKC/SBK keys; fuse burning is irreversible; three PKC keys can be fused and the first two revoked; RSA-3K and ECDSA P-256/P-521 (RSA-2048 unsupported on Orin); UEFI Secure Boot enabled at flash cannot be disabled without reflashing; A/B kernel images must be signed with the db key.

Jetson Orin disk encryption (r36.4.4): LUKS AES-XTS-256; the OP-TEE luks-srv TA derives a per-device passphrase from the EKB disk-encryption key, ECID and disk UUID; mass-flashed generic keys are replaced per device at first boot.

Jetson Orin firmware TPM (r36.4.4): TPM 2.0 reference implementation as an OP-TEE TA with measured boot into PCRs; needs fused KDK0 and offline EK-certificate provisioning; online provisioning not yet available.

k3s hardening guide: audit logging is not enabled by default; the restricted Pod Security policy needs a flag and psa.yaml; 'By default, K3s does not include any pod security or network policies' although its controller enforces policies once created.
k3s documents SELinux support through the k3s-selinux RPM (CentOS example) and mentions AppArmor only for rootless mode.

Kubernetes AppArmor support is stable since 1.31 (appArmorProfile: RuntimeDefault/Localhost/Unconfined; profiles must be loaded on every node); Pod Security Standards Baseline notes that on supported hosts the RuntimeDefault AppArmor profile is applied by default.
SLSA v1.2 is the approved current spec (v1.1 retired); Build L1 = provenance exists, L2 = hosted build platform with signed provenance, L3 = hardened build platform.
GitHub artifact attestations provide SLSA v1.0 Build Level 2 by default and Level 3 when builds run in an isolated reusable workflow; they use Sigstore.
Cosign docs: the new protobuf bundle format supports offline verification; signatures can also be verified against an on-disk public key (cosign verify --key).

OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection: 'it is unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention'; mitigations include least privilege, handling sensitive functions in code, human approval for high-risk actions, and segregating external content.

MCP Security Best Practices (spec 2025-11-25): token passthrough is forbidden (servers MUST NOT accept tokens not issued to them); confused-deputy proxies MUST do per-client consent; one-click local servers MUST show the exact command and get consent and SHOULD be sandboxed; progressive least-privilege scopes.

CaMeL ('Defeating Prompt Injections by Design', arXiv:2503.18813v2) separates control flow from untrusted data and enforces capabilities at tool calls, solving 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security versus 84% undefended.
MAVLink 2 message signing authenticates message origin using a 32-byte shared secret and a 48-bit truncated SHA-256 signature; the page describes signing only, not encryption.
